concept_sheet: C6 — The Keyspace Decision (brainstorm sheet, tier T3 Advanced)

deliverables.text: A keyspace table for The Long Wall's nominal password, The Second Gate's nominal password, and the accounts-payable system's reduced effective password — character-set size, password length, and total possible passwords computed by the Fundamental Counting Principle, with the full application of the principle shown for at least one row.

A time-to-crack table converting each of the three keyspaces from D1 into an expected time to crack, in years, at the sourced offline guessing rate, with the full compound-unit conversion shown for at least one row.

A collision-bound analysis of the accounts-payable system's reduced keyspace: using the Pigeonhole Principle, find the minimum number of employees who would have to share that reduced keyspace before two are guaranteed to hold the identical accounts-payable password, and compare that number to Bramwell's actual employee count.

A breach-vector table showing the share of real-world account takeovers attributable to credential theft/phishing versus direct password guessing, and the published rate at which a second authentication factor blocks account takeover even when the attacker already holds a correct password, combined into a single expected-annual-takeover figure for each standard.

A cost-per-dollar synthesis table combining D2's time-to-crack figures, D4's breach-vector-weighted takeover figures, and each standard's annual implementation and support cost into the case's primary metric — expected time-to-crack, in years, per dollar of implementation and support cost — for both standards, with the full arithmetic shown.

balance.argument_a: A fourteen-character password drawn from a 70-character set is brute-force-infeasible by any realistic measure -- exhausting its keyspace takes an expected 1.55 x 10^13 years at the sourced benchmark rate. The cost is modest ($60/employee/year) and mostly one-time tooling. If the threat that matters is an attacker guessing offline against stolen hashes, The Long Wall ends the conversation before it starts.
balance.argument_b: Real account takeovers overwhelmingly do not happen via brute-force guessing: credential abuse (stolen, phished, or reused passwords) appears somewhere in the chain of 39% of real breaches (S2), and none of that channel cares how long the password is. A second factor defends that channel directly, cutting takeover risk by 98.56% even when the attacker already has a correct password (S3). Weighted by how real attackers actually get in, The Second Gate comes out ahead on the case's own primary metric, and at a lower dollar cost per employee ($36 vs $60).
balance.margin_basis: For each option: combine the annual probability of compromise via direct password guessing (1 / D2 crack-time) and via the credential-abuse channel (Appendix E MA3's stated annual attempt rate, unmitigated for A, reduced by S3's 98.56% for B), weighted 61%/39% by S2's vulnerability-exploitation/credential-abuse split; invert to expected years to compromise; divide by each option's annual per-employee cost (Appendix D). Option A: ~320.5 years / $60.00 = 5.34 years/$. Option B: ~214.0 years / $36.00 = 5.94 years/$. Option B wins by 10.1%.
balance.the_trap: D2 alone (raw brute-force crack time with no breach-vector weighting) makes Option A appear to win by a factor of roughly 70 billion on the same nominal metric -- a number large enough that a Hero who stops at D2 will report it with total, misplaced confidence. The whole case is discovering that this naive computation is the wrong one; D4's weighting is not optional texture, it is the deliverable that actually decides the dilemma. See RESEARCH_LOG.md 'A note on the metric redesign' for the full derivation showing why the raw metric can never be close (a 6-character password-length gap on a fixed 70-symbol alphabet produces a ~70^6 ~= 1.17x10^11 keyspace ratio regardless of attack rate or cost -- a mathematical inevitability, not a tunable parameter).

cohort_bands.note: The Socratic plan runs as written. Split the room into two policy desks for the Data Deep Dive -- one builds D1/D2 for The Long Wall, one for The Second Gate -- and have them trade tables before D4/D5.
Anchors 2 and 3 combine into one pass. Run one deep-conflict thread only. Do not split into two desks; work one keyspace together on the board and leave the rest as homework.

No vote at Anchor 1 -- the learner states an initial position, and the guide argues the other side directly. Skip the deep-conflict threads and spend the recovered time on D3, the pigeonhole bound, which is the least intuitive step to do alone.

sensitivity_disclosure.justification: No public source states an annual per-account successful-compromise rate for this specific event; the true rate exists at Bramwell (and at any real company) but is not publicly measured or disclosed. The stated 0.008 is a documented good-faith estimate anchored to the closest public analogue -- commonly cited employee phishing-susceptibility (click-through) rates -- set deliberately below them because susceptibility overstates completed compromise. Tier 2 probe 5 finds the primary metric's verdict flips under a -50% swing on this parameter and the 20% balance cap breaks in both directions; this is a genuine, disclosed instability, not a scoping bug, and it is the case's intended fault line (see case.md Appendix E MA3 and FACILITATOR.md's Socratic questions/trap).

No independently verifiable per-employee help-desk cost figure exists for a 14-character minimum's forgotten-password rate; the widely repeated '$70 per reset' figure traces to Forrester Research but no dated primary publication stating it could be located, so it was excluded as unsourced (see RESEARCH_LOG.md). The stated $12.00 is a documented, modest placeholder chosen to sit well below the excluded figure and below the sourced $48 password-manager base cost it adds to. Tier 2 probe 5 finds a +50% swing on this parameter breaks the 20% balance cap (22.4%) without flipping the verdict; disclosed here rather than retuned, since no genuine retune of this or the MA3 assumption can satisfy both a base margin under the cap and stability under a +/-50% swing without gutting the metric's intended sensitivity to Appendix E's stated assumptions.

modeling_assumptions.basis: Bramwell is fictional. 400 sits in the middle of the commonly used 100-999 employee band for 'mid-size company.'
modeling_assumptions.sensitivity: Scales both options' total dollar cost identically (D5's per-employee metric is unaffected) and scales D3's pigeonhole comparison headcount proportionally. Does not change which option wins D5's per-employee metric.

modeling_assumptions.assumption: Fraction of Bramwell's employees whose accounts touch the accounts-payable legacy system
modeling_assumptions.basis: No real company's finance-system access list is public; 20% is a plausible finance/accounts-payable-adjacent share for a mid-size firm.
modeling_assumptions.sensitivity: Directly sets the headcount D3 compares against the pigeonhole guarantee threshold. Because that threshold (2,821,109,907,457) exceeds any plausible employee count by nine to eleven orders of magnitude, no realistic value of MA2 changes D3's conclusion.

modeling_assumptions.assumption: Annual rate at which a given employee account experiences a successful credential-theft or phishing-based compromise attempt
modeling_assumptions.basis: No public source states an annual per-account success rate for this specific event. Deliberately conservative -- well below commonly cited employee phishing-susceptibility rates, which describe click-throughs rather than completed credential theft. The case's most load-bearing, least certain dial, stated openly rather than buried in D5's table.
modeling_assumptions.sensitivity: The primary metric weights the credential-abuse channel directly by this rate, so the final comparison is sensitive to this value. The case's most load-bearing, least certain dial.

modeling_assumptions.assumption: The Long Wall's incremental annual help-desk cost per employee, beyond password-manager licensing, from a higher forgotten-password rate under a 14-character minimum
modeling_assumptions.basis: No independently verifiable per-employee figure exists (the commonly repeated '$70 per reset' figure traces to Forrester Research but no dated, primary Forrester publication stating it could be located and fetched, so it is excluded as unsourced). $12 is a stated, modest placeholder value, deliberately small relative to the sourced $48 password-manager cost it sits beside.
modeling_assumptions.sensitivity: Adds linearly to The Long Wall's per-employee cost ($48 + MA4). The final comparison is sensitive to this value, since it moves Option A's cost denominator directly.
